name: Inulin and inulin-type fructans
short: Case reports: anaphylactic shock after inulin-containing foods. Inulin/sinistrin medicines withdrawn in France after serious allergic reactions, one fatal. Trials: gas, bloating. Mice: liver cancer.
text: Serious allergic reactions to inulin are documented in case reports: a woman with a past allergy to artichoke had two immediate allergic reactions, one of them a severe anaphylactic shock, after eating two types of health foods containing inulin, and IgE antibodies specific to inulin were identified; a letter is titled as a report of anaphylaxis from inulin in vegetables and processed food. Separately, in 2018 the French medicines agency withdrew pharmaceutical products containing inulin and its analogue sinistrin after several reports of serious hypersensitivity reactions, including a fatal outcome; a pharmacovigilance study counted 134 adverse reactions to these products registered from 1991 to 2018, 47% classed as serious and 96% hypersensitivity reactions, apparently associated with batches of sinistrin, and in one clinical trial 4 of 163 participants had hypersensitivity reactions, including one anaphylactic shock; the same study observed no adverse reactions in current use at a hospital and said that in the literature, reactions to inulin and sinistrin are very rarely reported and mostly benign. Those were medicinal products, not food or supplement inulin; the study abstract does not state the route, and a separate case report describes anaphylaxis after intravenous inulin used to measure kidney function (the title names the product as sinistrin, the inulin analogue). With inulin taken by mouth, gastrointestinal effects are the commonly reported harm: in randomised crossover trials in healthy adults, chicory inulin and oligofructose tended to increase gastrointestinal symptoms mildly, most often flatulence then bloating, while the higher of two oligofructose doses substantially increased symptoms compared with control, and agave inulin slightly increased bloating, flatulence and rumbling without increasing diarrhoea. In a blinded crossover challenge (7 days on each diet) in 59 people with self-reported non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, fructans (source not stated in the abstract) produced significantly higher overall symptom and bloating scores than gluten; mean scores with fructans were also higher than with placebo (overall 38.6 vs 34.3; bloating 11.6 vs 10.1), but the abstract reports no separate test of fructans against placebo, and 24 participants had their highest overall score after fructans against 22 after placebo (and 13 after gluten). In animal studies, adding inulin to the diet induced liver cancer in several strains of mice with disturbed gut bacteria and, combined with a high-fat diet, in normal mice, and the authors urged great caution about enriching foods with fermentable fibre; in another mouse study inulin worsened chemically induced colitis, and an inulin-enriched diet in mothers during lactation increased their offspring's susceptibility to colitis. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
